full_article:
Key Takeaways:

Nepal issues three-day high alert over Cyclone Arnab

Five provinces expected to face the strongest impacts

Heavy snowfall snowstorms and avalanche risks forecast in Himalayan areas

Road air travel and daily activities could face disruptions

Nepal has issued a high-alert advisory for October 29-31 as Cyclone Arnab, expected to make landfall in India, could bring heavy rain, thunderstorms, strong winds and snowfall across large parts of the country.

Related Articles Heavy rain, thunderstorms forecast in several provinces today Windstorms, heavy rain forecast across several provinces

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) warned that the cyclone's impacts are likely to be felt from the night of October 29, with Koshi, Madhesh, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces expected to face the greatest effects on October 30 and 31.

Forecasters say moderate rainfall accompanied by thunder, lightning and strong winds is likely in many places, while heavy rainfall is possible in some areas. Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces could also experience rain and thunderstorms, with isolated heavy downpours.

title: Nepal Supreme Court orders dedicated data protection law for national ID - Biometric Update
description: Nepal Supreme Court orders dedicated data protection law for national ID  Biometric Update
publisher.title: Biometric Update
full_article:
The Supreme Court of Nepal has directed the government to draft a dedicated law governing the privacy and security of personal and biometric data collected through the country’s National Identity Card (NID) program. Nepal’s highest court cited concerns that existing safeguards are insufficient.

In a ruling issued on 9 October, the court said constitutional protections for privacy require a comprehensive legal framework approved by Parliament, rather than relying on administrative standards and committees.

The court also struck down a Nepal Rastra Bank directive that had made the National Identity Card the sole basis for opening or renewing bank accounts. The ruling states that citizens should not be denied access to banking services because they do not possess a National Identity Card.

The judges argued that biometric data such as fingerprints and retinal scans are highly sensitive and that any compromise could have lasting consequences for both individuals and national security, according to Setopati.

The court also warned against allowing private banks broad access to biometric records, calling instead for verification systems that return only a yes-or-no response.

The case was brought by advocate Sarita Adhikari, who challenged requirements allowing banks to verify customers through NID-linked biometric records. She argued that the absence of a clear legal framework governing access to, use of and retention of biometric data violated constitutional privacy rights.

The government argued that a Data Security Committee and standards developed under the National Identity Card and Registration Act already provided safeguards, but the court found them inadequate.

The court called for a standalone Data Protection Act that would clearly define data collection purposes, usage limits, citizens’ rights, oversight mechanisms, penalties and remedies for violations.

The ruling raises questions about expanding mandatory national ID use without stronger safeguards for personal and biometric data, particularly when private organizations are involved in verification.

The country has recently required citizens aged 16 and older to use their national ID to enrol in, renew and access services under the country’s health insurance program from December 16.

title: Nepal Halts Himalayan Trekking Permits Amid Avalanche Risks - NDTV

full_article:
Nepal's Department of Immigration has suspended the issuance of trekking permits for restricted areas in high-hill and Himalayan regions for October 29–31, citing a high risk of heavy snowfall, snowstorms and avalanches.

The decision follows a warning by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority urging tourists to avoid travelling to these areas during the three days.

A special post-monsoon bulletin issued by the Nepal Meteorological Department said earlier that Cyclone Arnab in the Bay of Bengal was gaining strength and was expected to bring heavy rainfall, strong winds and a high risk of snowfall and avalanches across several parts of the Himalayan country.

In a statement, the Department of Immigration, which issues trekking permits to foreign nationals visiting restricted areas, also urged trekkers who had already obtained permits for restricted areas in high-hill and Himalayan regions to suspend their treks during the period to minimise potential risks.

title: Movie Review: In 'Everest: The Other Side,' tragedy and triumph intermingle on the peaks of Nepal - Yahoo
description: Movie Review: In 'Everest: The Other Side,' tragedy and triumph intermingle on the peaks of Nepal  Yahoo
publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
Hike up and ski down was Jim Morrison's relatively straightforward dream, albeit not on your typical ski hill.

Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson aspired to summit Mount Everest's north side, something only five people had ever done. None had ever skied down it. Given the long stream of mountaineers that queue up on the south face, you could call it the most drastic feat ever of avoiding a lift line.

"Everest: The Other Side," by "Free Solo" filmmakers Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin, is the big-screen chronicle of Morrison and Nelson's mission. Theirs is a quixotic aspiration: climb the world's highest peak and then coast down.

But "Everest: The Other Side" is as much a document of tragedy and grief as it is one of extreme sport. On a similar expedition in 2022 while biding their time for Everest, Morrison and Nelson — partners in love and adventure — reached the top of a Nepalese mountain. But after just a few turns on her skis, a sheet of snow dislodged underneath Nelson. She died in the avalanche.

Nelson's death reverberated through the mountaineering world and it reshaped the film Vasarhelyi and Chin were making. In "Free Solo," which documents Alex Honnold ascending El Capitan in Yosemite without ropes or a harness, the filmmakers had to contemplate the possibility that Honnold might fall to his death.

In "Everest," that awful possibility comes to pass. Nelson's fatal fall, as well as Morrison's recovery of her body two days later, is captured with agonizing IMAX clarity. If "Free Solo" was about an unmitigated triumph, "Everest" wrestles with a darker side of such perilous exploits.

"This movie, the worst happened," Vasarhelyi says in a brief moment on screen.

Risk tolerance is a common topic for Vasarhelyi and Chin, filmmakers who have intrepidly fused nature documentaries with adventure drama. Chin is himself a decorated climber; he summited and skied down the south face of Everest in 2006.

But in "Everest," questioning whether it's worth it is front and center. The movie lingers on the moments when Morrison and his team leave their homes, parting with children for two-month stints during which they'll risk their lives on desolate peaks on the other side of the world. When Nelson dies, she leaves behind two boys. As the years tick on in the documentary, we watch them grow up without their mother.

Yet within months of her death, Morrison, from his lakeside Tahoe home, resolves to push ahead with the Everest climb. Tragedy isn't new to him. Years earlier, he lost his wife, Katie, and two children, Wyatt and Hannah, in a plane crash. After first finding a walk down the driveway an insurmountable hike, Morrison resolves to live for them.

So his aim to reach the top of Everest and ski down may be a daredevil feat, but it's also a grieving, heavy-hearted quest. He describes his yearning to ride down "the raddest ski line in the world." But what's compelling him is also something that can't be easily articulated.

"Everest: The Other Side" is, to a certain extent, alive to these quandaries. The filmmakers even share in them. Chin accompanies Morrison on both an aborted ascent and the successful attempt in 2025.

Deciding to continue with the project is its own debate for Chin and Vasarhelyi. They have two children of their own. Their proximity to extreme expeditions has already brought tragedy close to home. "How many people who have eaten at our dinner table have died?" Vasarhelyi asks him. The couple divorced in 2025, though their separation goes unmentioned in the film.

While these debates are often present in the documentary, "Everest: The Other Side" grows increasingly shy of them. The higher Morrison climbs, the less inquisitive the movie gets. On the first attempted ascent, some of the Sherpas grow wary of the risks involved. Their sensible hesitations don't put Morrison, handsomely outfitted by his North Face sponsor, in the best light.

By the time Morrison realizes his dream, it feels as though many have, off camera, moved on with their lives. The families back home fall out of the movie. "Everest: The Other Side" becomes a mournful and increasingly solitary march.

Maybe that's appropriate. Morrison's extreme compulsion inevitably pulls him away from us, leaving behind a more disquieting film. Even he can't help but notice while hiking up that the snow conditions he'll be skiing down are rock hard and terrible. The descent, lasting four hours, is a feat of skill, perseverance and bravery. Even on a bad day, he'd have to grant, the skiing would have been better back home.

"Everest: The Other Side," a Walt Disney Co. release in theaters Friday, is rated PG-13 by the Motion Picture Association for thematic material and brief strong language. Running time: 115 minutes. Two and a half stars out of four.
